prompt:
Use case: illustration-story.
Create a square watercolor storyboard, ideally 1536×1536, exactly TWO columns by THREE rows, six independent 3:2 LANDSCAPE panels in row-major order. Equal cells with a narrow clear ivory paper gap, no borders, labels or frames; no scene crosses a cell boundary. Keep the full primary subject inside the central 82% of each cell.
MEDIUM ONLY is shared: sophisticated adult editorial watercolor on warm ivory cold-pressed paper, transparent layered washes, expressive pencil contours, irregular pigment edges softly dissolving into unpainted paper. Sage, terracotta, lavender, soft ochre with scene-appropriate blues and greens. Loose believable anatomy and gestures, not photographic, not 3D, not cartoon. Warm and adult, but do NOT impose golden sunshine or a cozy room on every setting.
Each panel illustrates the SPECIFIC QUESTION supplied, not merely the topic. Make the action or idea readable without a caption. Change the subject, action, setting, scale or viewpoint substantially for every panel. A close crop of a prop from the preceding scene is not a new concept. Use the concrete directions below, no decorative filler or invented extra scenes.
Fictional adults and natural hands/gestures are welcome where specified; use candid back/side/over-shoulder views or crop naturally above the chin, never blank faceless heads. No idealized romance, no default gender roles, no recognizable real person. Adults of ordinary appearance, varied skin tones. These are fictional examples, not reconstructions of a user's memories. Emotion can be mixed; do not visually assert reconciliation or a promised outcome.
STRICTLY NO cups, mugs, drinking glasses, plates, cutlery, kettles, table settings, flower vases, decorative bouquets, hearts, rings, floating icons, puzzle metaphors, UI, captions, letters, numbers, handwriting, logos or watermarks. No café, Tuscan room or wicker furniture unless expressly requested. Book pages, maps, tickets and screens must have no readable writing. Do not fill unrelated panels with the same furniture, fabric or object.
Use an ordinary adult couple in their forties, one with short dark hair and one with short graying hair, different skin tones. Both have equal dignity; no villain or aggressor. Do not gender the temperature preferences.
STORY S09: The small thing we get stuck on
PANEL 1
Question context (do not render as text): What small thing do we keep getting stuck on?
Recognition cue: A recurring small clash
Paint: Two adult hands reach toward the same plain room thermostat from different sides, one sleeve heavy and one sleeve light; the dial has only a cool-blue and warm-rust arc, no numbers or text. An instantly recognizable small disagreement about temperature.
PANEL 2
Question context (do not render as text): Think of the last time that came up. What mattered to you then?
Recognition cue: What mattered to me then
Paint: One adult sits at a work corner wearing a cardigan and warming cold hands near their sleeves, the thermostat faintly visible beyond. Their bodily comfort and own perspective are central, no blame or villain.
PANEL 3
Question context (do not render as text): What do you wish I had understood in that moment?
Recognition cue: The part I wish you understood
Paint: From the other side of the same room, an adult in light clothing rolls up sleeves and pushes hair away from a warm forehead while trying to concentrate. A different lived experience behind the same small clash, shown kindly.
PANEL 4
Question context (do not render as text): What could we say if that talk starts to feel tense?
Recognition cue: A way to pause a tense talk
Paint: Two adults face each other at comfortable distance; one gently lifts an open palm asking for a pause while the other lowers their own hands and takes a breath. Calm human gesture, no anger, pointing fingers, damage or reconciliation hug.
PANEL 5
Question context (do not render as text): What is one small thing we could try when that issue comes up again?
Recognition cue: One small possible change
Paint: A standing fan and a light throw are set as two available options near the room's plain thermostat, with an adult's hand hovering undecided toward the controls. A small experiment available, not a declared solution or perfect agreement.
PANEL 6
Question context (do not render as text): If you like, keep one thing you want me to understand. We can leave the issue open.
Recognition cue: We can leave the issue open
Paint: Two adults stand side by side looking at the same thermostat, still dressed for different comfort needs, hands relaxed and space between them. The issue can rest without a visual verdict.
